reason: The chapter's top-ranked candidate and a genuine KJV singleton — “creation of the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and it should still be declined. The singleton is arithmetic rather than distinctive: the King James Bible's ordinary idiom for the same idea is 'the foundation of the world', which it writes ten times, and it simply had occasion to write 'creation of the world' once. Romans 1:20 is an argument that God's invisible attributes are inferable from created things, and it uses the phrase adverbially, 'from the creation of the world', meaning ever since. Ether 1:3 uses it as the title of a section of a record — 'the first part of this record, which speaketh concerning the creation of the world, and also of Adam'. Nothing else of Romans 1 is anywhere near. If anything the verse tells against KJV dependence at this point, since it reaches for the collocation the KJV almost never uses.

'And Ahah was the son of Seth', matched against 'which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam'. The Luke 3 contact is real and is adjudicated in this chapter, but not here: the case rests on the ascending form of the whole genealogy (link at 1:6) and on the one clause that adopts Luke's relative construction (link at 1:32). At 1:10 the shared words are a name the Book of Mormon needs for its own list and the four-word chain 'was the son of', which stands in 23 KJV verses. A reader sent here by the machine should read the rows at 1:6 and 1:32. The same disposal covers the 1 Samuel 14:51 match at 1:19 — see that entry.

'And Kish was the son of Corom', matched against 'And Kish was the father of Saul; and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel.' A four-word run with a proper name in it, which is why it ranked, and the name is the whole of the resemblance. Saul's father Kish is a Benjaminite whose sole narrative function is to lose the asses that send his son to Samuel; Ether's Kish is the twelfth name up a Jaredite king-list and has no story attached at this point in the record at all. The verses agree because both are genealogical notices containing a Kish, and the KJV happens to phrase its notice with the same four function words the Book of Mormon uses twenty-five times in this chapter. This entry also covers the general question of whether the chapter's formula is the Chronicler's: 1 Chronicles 6:33-38 and Ezra 7:1-5 do run ascending 'son of' chains, but they are verbless appositions — 'the son of Joel, the son of Shemuel' — and Ether 1 uses a finite clause each time. The form is argued at 1:6 and the one verbal agreement is at 1:32.

sharedText: scattered upon all the face of the earth
reason: A nine-word run, the longest in the chapter, and a genuine KJV singleton — but it is the Book of Mormon's own dispersion formula, adjudicated as a composite element at 1 Nephi 10:12 and excluded as a repeat at 1 Nephi 13:39, 1 Nephi 14:14, 3 Nephi 5:24, 3 Nephi 21:24 and elsewhere; the standing exclusion filed in 1 Nephi covers it. What is worth recording is what happens here and nowhere else in the corpus. This is the one verse in the Book of Mormon that narrates the event the formula describes, and at that verse the formula displaces its own scriptural source: Genesis 11:8 and 11:9 both read 'scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth', and Ether 1:33, in a sentence that has just quoted Genesis 11:9's 'confound the language', writes 'scattered upon all the face of the earth' instead — Ezekiel's word order, and the corpus's. The verse takes its event from Genesis and its words for the event from its own house style. The link at this verse is Genesis 11:9; see also Psalm 95:11 for the oath clause.

sharedText: a large and a mighty man
reason: The brother of Jared is introduced as 'a large and a mighty man', and the Genesis chapter immediately preceding the tower gives the only mighty man of the region: 'And Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth' (10:8). The temptation is strong and the setting is right. But 'mighty man' is one of the KJV's commonest epithets, standing in dozens of verses, and Genesis 10:8-9 reads 'a mighty one' and 'a mighty hunter before the LORD' — not 'a mighty man' — while 'large' has no counterpart at all. The Nimrod material belongs to Ether 2:1, where the valley of Nimrod is named outright and where Hardy's apparatus keys Genesis 10:8-9; it is adjudicated there and not here.

A five-word run of pure connective tissue. 'It may be that' stands in eight KJV verses and Paul's is about wintering at Corinth. The verse's real business is the intercession formula, which is adjudicated at 1:38 against Joel 2:14 and Jonah 3:9 and which takes 1:36's 'turn away his anger' as its first half.

Five words spanning a clause boundary in both verses — Ether's 'inquire of the Lord whether he will drive us out', Paul's 'shall he receive of the Lord, whether he be bond or free'. The 'whether' governs different things and no content word is shared. Batched with it: 2 Kings 3:11's 'enquire of the LORD that we may', which is the KJV's standard oracle-seeking formula (Genesis 25:22, 1 Samuel 9:9, 1 Kings 22:5 and a dozen more) and identifies no source. The link at this verse is Hebrews 11:8.

Five words of KJV connective phrasing, in a verse about the passover of the resident alien. 'According to the word of the Lord' and its variants run through the whole Book of Mormon; covered by the standing boilerplate exclusion.

sharedText: it came to pass that the Lord
reason: A seven-word run and the top candidate at this verse; it is 'and it came to pass', which is the type case of the standing exclusion filed at 1 Nephi 2:1. Joshua 1:1 shares nothing else with the Lord's hearing of the brother of Jared.

A genuine KJV singleton — “both male and female” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and the sense is exactly opposed, which is what makes it worth an entry rather than silence. Numbers 5:3 is the law of the camp: 'Both male and female shall ye put out, without the camp shall ye put them; that they defile not their camps.' The phrase there governs expulsion of the unclean. In Ether 1:41 it governs the gathering-in of livestock for a voyage. Same four words, opposite direction of travel, and the machine ranked it first because the string is unique. The inventory Ether 1:41 is actually reproducing is Noah's, Genesis 6:19-21, where the creatures are 'male and female' and come 'after their kind' and food is gathered; the link is written there. The Genesis 7:16 candidate at the same verse — “male and female of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — is superseded by the same row, which takes 6:19-21 as the source because Ether follows the loading command and not the boarding notice.

Four words, and in Genesis they introduce the curse on the serpent while in Ether they mark the completion of an obedient errand. The KJV writes 'because thou hast done this' at Genesis 3:14 and Genesis 22:16 with opposite valuations, which is a fair measure of how little the string carries. Batched with the same verse's Joel 3:2 match, 'down into the valley': the phrase stands in exactly two KJV verses and Joel's is the valley of Jehoshaphat, a place of judgment on gathered nations, where Ether's is a nameless valley northward that is a stage on a journey. The link at this verse is Micah 2:13.

sharedText: and there will I meet thee
reason: Worth recording because it is the kind of near-miss a careful reader will notice and the register should be seen to have noticed. Ether 1:42 has God appoint a rendezvous — 'And there will I meet thee' — and the KJV has a formula for God appointing a rendezvous: “there I will meet with thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 25:22, with 'where I will meet with thee' at Exodus 30:6 and 30:36 and 'there I will meet with you' at Exodus 29:42-43. But that formula is the sanctuary formula without exception: every occurrence is the mercy seat, the altar of incense or the door of the tabernacle, and it means the place where God will be permanently available to Moses, not a place to be at on a particular day. Ether's is a map reference. The word order differs too — 'there will I meet thee' against 'there I will meet with thee' — and the preposition the KJV never omits is omitted. Declined.

The chapter's second-ranked candidate at this verse and its direction is reversed: “will I bless thee” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 63:4 and Psalm 145:2, and in both of them the speaker blessing is the worshipper and the one blessed is God. Ether 1:43 is God blessing a man. The clause belongs to the Abrahamic promise adjudicated at this verse against Genesis 12:2, where the KJV reads 'and I will bless thee'. Batched with the remaining machine candidates at 1:43, none of which shares a content word that construes: Leviticus 20:23 on 'the nation which I', Genesis 17:7 on 'thee and thy seed' (a real element of the promise, but the promise is fixed on Genesis 12:2 by the great-nation clause), Ezekiel 7:27 on 'I will do unto', Daniel 1:3 on 'seed and of the', Ezra 9:15 on 'thee because of this', and Ezekiel 34:6's dispersion formula for the fourth time in the chapter — see the entry at 1:33.
